articles.title: Pars Plana Vitrectomy for Inadvertent Intravitreal Injection of Hyaluronic Acid Dermal Filler: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal fillers are commonly used in cosmetic practice and are generally safe; however, ocular complications may occur if material is introduced into periocular or intraocular structures. Although vascular-related vision loss has been widely reported, direct intravitreal dermal filler deposition is exceedingly rare, and subsequent management with vitrectomy has not been previously documented. This report presents the clinical course and management of inadvertent intravitreal injection of HA filler and highlights considerations for safe removal.

articles.title: Adjunctive topical bromfenac and the 3-year bevacizumab injection burden in macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion.
articles.abstract: Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy for macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) imposes a substantial long-term injection burden. We evaluated whether eyes prescribed adjunctive topical bromfenac required fewer intravitreal bevacizumab injections over 3 years than those receiving bevacizumab monotherapy.

articles.title: Case Report: Histamine-mediated inflammation and mast cell modulation in central serous chorioretinopathy: a two case illustrations.
articles.abstract: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) is characterized by retinal pigment epithelium dysfunction and choroidal hyperpermeability. Beyond established associations such as psychosocial stress and corticosteroid exposure, experimental and epidemiological findings raise the possibility that mast cell and histamine-related pathways may contribute to CSCR pathophysiology. This study reviews mechanistic and clinical evidence for the role of histamine in the pathogenesis of CSCR, as well as the role of histamine-targeted therapies in this condition. We also present two cases, highlighting the possible therapeutic role of anti-allergy agents in CSCR.

articles.title: When Erectile Dysfunction Therapy Clouds the Vision: Central Serous Chorioretinopathy after Sildenafil in a Healthy Male.
articles.abstract: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) is a pachychoroid-spectrum disorder characterized by serous neurosensory retinal detachment secondary to choroidal vascular congestion and retinal pigment epithelial dysfunction. While corticosteroid use and psychological stress are well-established risk factors, phosphodiesterase type-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil citrate, widely used for erectile dysfunction, have been increasingly recognized as an under-reported pharmacological trigger, with proposed mechanisms involving acute choroidal vasodilation and hyperpermeability. A 39-year-old previously healthy male presented with sudden, painless diminution of vision in the right eye of 48 h, occurring shortly after ingestion of a single large recreational dose of sildenafil citrate. Best-corrected visual acuity was reduced to 6/18 in the right eye, with a normal left eye. Fundus examination revealed a well-demarcated serous macular elevation, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) confirmed a dome-shaped neurosensory detachment with a markedly elevated central subfield thickness. A comprehensive systemic and hematological workup, including thrombophilia screening and cardiac evaluation, was unremarkable, supporting a diagnosis of sildenafil-induced CSCR. The patient was managed conservatively with topical nepafenac, topical Flurbiprofen, and oral alcaftadine, along with cessation of further sildenafil use. Serial follow-up over approximately 2 months demonstrated progressive resolution of subretinal fluid, normalization of central subfield thickness, and preservation of visual acuity, with OCT angiography confirming adequate perfusion and no neovascular complication. This case reinforces sildenafil as a potential, dose-related precipitant of acute CSCR even after a single high dose in patients without conventional risk factors. Prompt recognition, drug cessation, and conservative management resulted in complete anatomical and visual recovery, highlighting the importance of a thorough medication history in young patients presenting with unexplained central visual disturbance.

articles.title: Hemorrhagic Occlusive Retinal Vasculitis After Therapeutic Intravitreal Vancomycin with Favorable Recovery Following Early Vitrectomy: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: To describe a postoperative case most consistent with vancomycin-associated hemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis (HORV) in which early pars plana vitrectomy (PPV), undertaken for presumed endophthalmitis, proved diagnostically decisive, with a favorable visual outcome.

articles.title: Advancing nanomaterials for treatment of eye diseases: a review.
articles.abstract: Ocular diseases involving both the anterior and posterior segments-such as dry eye disease, keratitis, glaucoma, cataracts, diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, and ocular tumors-remain major contributors to global visual impairment. Conventional topical and systemic therapies are limited by rapid clearance, restricted penetration across ocular barriers, and poor bioavailability, particularly for posterior-segment targets. Nanotechnology has introduced a transformative therapeutic paradigm by enabling controlled pharmacokinetics, enhanced tissue penetration, and site-specific delivery. A wide range of engineered nanomaterials-including polymeric nanoparticles, lipid-based carriers, dendrimers, metallic and metal-oxide nanoparticles, mesoporous silica systems, cerium oxide nanozymes, carbon quantum dots, nanogels, and electrospun nanofibers-has demonstrated improved drug loading, sustained release, ocular surface retention, and compatibility with biologics and gene-based agents. Emerging minimally invasive platforms, such as 4D printed smart scaffolds, dissolving microneedles and magnetically driven microrobots, further enable precise transscleral or intravitreal delivery, active navigation through the vitreous, and targeted interaction with retinal lesions. Parallel clinical advances, including FDA-approved nanoformulations and ongoing trials, confirm the translational potential of these technologies. Plus, artificial intelligence now accelerates both ophthalmic diagnosis and nanocarrier design, enabling predictive modeling of nano-bio interactions, personalized delivery strategies, and real-time disease assessment. This review integrates current advances in nanomaterial engineering and AI-guided innovation, outlining their convergent roles in shaping next-generation precision therapeutics for vision preservation and restoration.

articles.title: Combined central retinal and posterior ciliary artery occlusion in a young female with primary myelofibrosis and Sweet's syndrome: A case report.
articles.abstract: Primary myelofibrosis (PMF) is a rare myeloproliferative neoplasm that typically affects older adults but may present aggressively in younger patients. Thromboembolic complications are well recognized, though arterial occlusions are uncommon in this age group. Ocular ischemia associated with systemic inflammatory conditions such as Sweet's syndrome is exceedingly rare. A 22-year-old female with PMF, diagnosed 18 months earlier and managed initially with ruxolitinib, presented with sudden, complete loss of vision in her left eye. She also had a history of Sweet's syndrome managed with oral corticosteroids and had received multiple blood transfusions. Ophthalmic evaluation revealed no light perception in the left eye, a pale retina with attenuated vessels, and a cherry-red spot. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed hyperreflectivity of the inner retinal layers, and OCT angiography demonstrated markedly reduced perfusion in all vascular plexuses. Carotid Doppler, echocardiography, and ECG excluded embolic sources. Despite ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis, acetazolamide, and anticoagulation with apixaban, vision did not recover. One week later, she developed anterior uveitis, keratic precipitates, and elevated intraocular pressure. Fundus showed Amalric's sign of choroidal infarction and Elschnig spots, confirmed on fluorescein angiography. Inflammation responded to topical and systemic corticosteroids, with normalization of intraocular pressure. This is the first documented case of combined central retinal artery occlusion and posterior ciliary artery occlusion with anterior uveitis in a young PMF patient with Sweet's syndrome. The case underscores the multifactorial contribution of hypercoagulability, systemic inflammation, and transfusion-related factors in ocular ischemia.

articles.title: Pharmacological and Safety Evaluation of the Small Molecule MP-004 Following Topical Ocular Administration for the Treatment of Inherited Retinal Dystrophies.
articles.abstract: MP-004 is a novel small molecule under development as a non-invasive therapeutic for inherited retinal dystrophies (IRDs), including retinitis pigmentosa. MP-004 halts photoreceptor degeneration by modulating calcium dysregulation and oxidative stress, two critical pathways involved in IRDs. Here, we evaluated its ocular concentration and safety profile following topical administration in three animal species (mouse, rabbit, and pig).

articles.title: Phenylboronate hydrogel for administration route tailored dual-drug delivery to anterior and posterior ocular segments.
articles.abstract: Frequent multidrug eyedrop instillation for ocular perioperative prophylaxis (e.g., cataract surgery) suffers from rapid nasolacrimal clearance, limited corneal penetration, and poor access to the posterior segment. To address these limitations, we engineered an interface-adaptive phenylboronate ester hydrogel for rapid in situ gelation and the co-entrapment of two frequently instilled drugs (moxifloxacin and dexamethasone) in their free or liposomal forms at physiological pH. This platform utilizes chemical crosslinking between hyaluronic acid-conjugated 2-aminophenylboronic acid and the diols of polyvinyl alcohol (HA-2APBA@PVA), forming a dynamic hydrogel network via phenylboronate ester bonds with a thermodynamically favorable formation energy (ΔG = -10.64 kcal/mol). This unique chemistry imparts shear-thinning injectability through fine ophthalmic needles, ensures mechanical stability against blink-induced shearing, and drives robust mucoadhesion with tear film mucins such as MUC5AC for prolonged ocular retention at the injection site. Architecturally, a "liposome-in-gel" system establishes hierarchical diffusion steps that suppress the initial burst effect and extend drug release duration by >2-fold compared to the free-drug solution control. The hydrogel demonstrates excellent ophthalmic compatibility, exhibiting physiological osmolality, >80% optical transmittance, and near 100% viability in human corneal and retinal pigment epithelial cells. Safety was further validated via Draize irritation testing and preserved ocular histology across topical and periocular administration routes. Unlike the rapid washout of standard eyedrops, this hydrogel depot ensures prolonged ocular surface retention. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed route-dependent versatility: compared to standard eyedrops, subconjunctival administration enhanced anterior segment exposure of moxifloxacin and dexamethasone by 14.9- and 8.6-fold, respectively, while sub-Tenon dosing facilitated targeted delivery to the posterior segment. This single, dynamic covalent chemistry provides a scalable, clinically compatible alternative strategy to eyedrops and advances multidrug therapies across both ocular segments.
